    Behind the figures

    What is calculated, and what is drawn.

    Everything moves by the Schwarzschild solution of Einstein’s equations: the spacetime outside a non-rotating, uncharged mass. Distances are in Schwarzschild radii rₛ (the radius of the horizon) and times in rₛ/c, the time light takes to cross one. The real-scale switch converts them for a black hole of one solar mass (rₛ ≈ 2.95 km) or for Sagittarius A* (about 4.3 million solar masses, rₛ ≈ 12.7 million km).

    dτ² = (1 − 1/r) dt² − dr² / (1 − 1/r) − r² dφ²

    Clocks

    A clock held still at r ticks at √(1 − 1/r) of the rate of a clock far away. This is not an illusion of signal delays: compare the clocks afterwards and the low one has aged less. No clock can be held still at or inside the horizon.

    Light and orbits

    Light rays and orbits are integrated exactly (fourth-order Runge–Kutta on the geodesic equations, with conserved energy and angular momentum). A ray’s direction is the direction measured by an observer held still where it starts. Light passing at less than 3√3/2 ≈ 2.6 rₛ from the centre (impact parameter) falls in; at 1.5 rₛ light can circle the hole. Circular orbits of matter are stable only outside 3 rₛ; orbits precess, by 2π / √(1 − 3/r) per lap for nearly circular ones.

    Time, and crossing the horizon

    The shared clock and figure 3 use Eddington–Finkelstein time t̃ = t + ln|r − 1|. Far away it ticks exactly like Schwarzschild time t, but unlike t it stays finite at the horizon, so a falling probe can be followed through it. In these coordinates ingoing light always moves at one unit of r per unit of t̃, and the outgoing edge of each light cone turns vertical at r = 1 and points inwards inside it.

    dt̃/dr = −1 (ingoing), (r + 1)/(r − 1) (outgoing)

    A probe dropped from rest falls on the exact cycloid r = R/2 (1 + cos η), τ = R3/2/2 (η + sin η): it crosses the horizon after a finite time on its own clock and reaches r = 0 soon after. Its signals are sent every 2 units of its own time and travel outwards along radial light rays; those sent from inside the horizon also move inwards.

    Touch and keys

    Space pause · R restart · 1–6 scenarios · scroll or + / − to zoom figure 1. Hover over anything for its numbers.

    Drawn for clarity: the size of clocks, probes and arrows, and the speed of the animation. Figure 1 is a snapshot at one value of t̃, so it shows light “now” in that slicing. Rotation, charge, tides and the hole’s growth are left out, and a real probe would be torn apart near a solar-mass hole well before the horizon (not near Sagittarius A*).

    Further reading: Taylor & Wheeler, Exploring Black Holes · Misner, Thorne & Wheeler, Gravitation, §31
